chapters.title: Secrets in Azure Key Vault
chapters.subtitle: Keep the secrets of your site in a vault

steps.text: Orchard Core can keep secrets in an Azure Key Vault, as well as in the database. In this video, you register a client in the host, configure the feature, create a secret in the vault, and read it from code.

The Secrets feature keeps secrets in the database. The Secrets - Azure Key Vault feature depends on it and adds a second store, which implements ISecretStore, is named AzureKeyVault, and keeps each secret as an entry in your vault.
Settings and code refer to a secret by name, so they do not depend on where it is kept. Enabling the feature moves nothing: existing secrets stay in the database.

chapters.title: Register the client
chapters.subtitle: The host owns the Azure connection

steps.text: The module never builds an Azure client. Your host registers a keyed SecretClient from a configuration section, and the service key can differ from the name of the section.

That section holds the address of the vault and the credential. Key Vault does not support API keys, so you choose a token credential, such as a managed identity, which needs no secret in the configuration.
For a client secret, use a secure configuration source, such as an environment variable, and not the settings file.

chapters.title: Configure the feature
chapters.subtitle: Point the store at your client

steps.text: In the Orchard Core configuration, AzureClient names the service key, and must match it exactly. A missing name, a key with no registered client, or the service key that the feature reserves for itself makes the store fail with an explicit error.
NamePrefix sets an application namespace, even for a site with one tenant. Use a distinct prefix for each application that shares a vault.

chapters.title: Create a secret in the vault
chapters.subtitle: Enable the feature, then choose the store

steps.text: Add the configuration before you enable the feature. Open Tools, Features, search for Key Vault, and select Enable next to Secrets - Azure Key Vault.
A message confirms that the feature was enabled. The Secrets pages are under Tools, Security.
On the Secrets page, select Add Secret, then Create under Text Secret. With two writable stores, the form has a Store list.
Enter a name and a value, choose AzureKeyVault as the store, and select Save.
The list shows the secret that you created, with a badge for its store. The database secret shows Database, and the form for a new secret refuses a name that either store already holds.
Open the vault secret again. Its store is fixed: to keep it in another store, use the Move action, which a separate video covers.

In the vault, the name of an entry is a readable, lowercase form of your prefix, the tenant name, and the secret name, plus a 24-character hash. Tags keep the exact prefix, tenant, name, and type, and the description if there is one.
The store lists only the entries that match the configured prefix and tenant. Changing the prefix, or renaming a tenant, changes the namespace, so earlier entries no longer appear.
A namespace is not an Azure authorization boundary: code with the vault credentials can read every entry. Use separate vaults for tenants that must not see each other's secrets.
Deleting a secret is a normal Key Vault delete. The module never purges, so the retention rules of the vault decide how long the value stays recoverable.

chapters.title: Use the vault from code
chapters.subtitle: Name the store, or share the client

steps.text: To read from the vault only, pass the store name to GetSecretAsync. A database entry then cannot hide a failed lookup in the vault.
To save to the vault, pass the store name to SaveSecretAsync. Without a store name, the secret goes to the default store, which is the database.
Your own services can use the same client: ask for a SecretClient with the FromKeyedServices attribute and the SecretClientServiceKey constant.

chapters.title: Develop locally
chapters.subtitle: An emulator instead of a vault

steps.text: For local development, the documentation configures the client for an Azure Key Vault emulator: a localhost address, an environment credential, and two flags that its local endpoints require.
Keep those flags in development configuration: both default to false, and production endpoints should leave them so. An emulator is never for production.
That is Azure Key Vault as a secret store: a client that your host registers, a short configuration, and the same secret names in the admin and in code. Thanks for watching.
